claim: The UK Biobank is a large population-based prospective cohort study enrolling more than 500,000 community-dwelling adults from 22 assessment centers across the UK between 2006 and 2010.
source: The UK Biobank is a large population-based prospective cohort study enrolling more than 500,000 community-dwelling adults from 22 assessment centers across the UK between 2006 and 2010 (Sudlow et al., 2015; Allen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sudlow et al., 2015 and Allen et al., 2012, which are referenced works describing the UK Biobank study design.

claim: Prediabetes affected approximately 720 million individuals worldwide in 2021, with a projection to 1 billion people by 2045.
source: Prediabetes affected approximately 720 million individuals worldwide in 2021, with a project to 1 billion people by 2045 (Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2022.

claim: Approximately 5–10% of people with prediabetes progress to having diabetes each year and the lifetime conversion rate to diabetes could be as high as 70%.
source: Approximately 5–10% of people with prediabetes progress to having diabetes each year and the lifetime conversion rate to diabetes could be as high as 70% (Tabák et al., 2012; Ligthart et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tabák et al., 2012 and Ligthart et al., 2016.

claim: Lifestyle modification and medical therapy have been proven to be effective in preventing or delaying the diabetes onset among people with prediabetes.
source: Although lifestyle modification and medical therapy have been proven to be effective in preventing or delaying the diabetes onset among people with prediabetes (Gong et al., 2019; DeFronzo et al., 2011; Herman, 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2019; DeFronzo et al., 2011; and Herman, 2023.

claim: The substantial cost of modification programs and medications as well as drug-related side effects limit the widespread delivery of such interventions in this large high-risk population.
source: the substantial cost of modification programs and medications as well as drug-related side effects limit the widespread delivery of such interventions in this large high-risk population (Roberts et al., 2017; Piller, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 2017 and Piller, 2019.

claim: A fraction of individuals with prediabetes may regress to normoglycemia without treatment.
source: Notably, the progression from prediabetes to diabetes is highly heterogeneous, and a fraction of individuals with prediabetes may regress to normoglycemia without treatment (Shang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shang et al., 2019.

claim: Fasting glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin A1c are convenient but less sensitive for risk stratification.
source: Glycemic indicators alone for risk stratification are deficient, with fasting glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) being convenient but less sensitive, while post-load glucose tolerance being sensitive but unfeasible in practice on a large scale (Phillips et al., 2014; Ferrannini, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Phillips et al., 2014 and Ferrannini, 2014.

claim: Post-load glucose tolerance is sensitive but unfeasible in practice on a large scale.
source: Glycemic indicators alone for risk stratification are deficient, with fasting glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) being convenient but less sensitive, while post-load glucose tolerance being sensitive but unfeasible in practice on a large scale (Phillips et al., 2014; Ferrannini, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Phillips et al., 2014 and Ferrannini, 2014.

claim: Several risk assessment models based on conventional clinical variables have been developed, but most of which had comparatively low performance and failed to take follow-up time into account.
source: In addition, several risk assessment models based on conventional clinical variables have been developed, but most of which had comparatively low performance and failed to take follow-up time into account (Yokota et al., 2017; Cahn et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yokota et al., 2017; Cahn et al., 2020; and Liang et al., 2021.

claim: Incorporating circulating metabolites into basic models with conventional risk factors could improve prediction of diabetes risk.
source: Previous studies have implied that incorporating circulating metabolites into basic models with conventional risk factors could improve prediction of diabetes risk (Merino et al., 2018; Peddinti et al., 2017; Rebholz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Merino et al., 2018; Peddinti et al., 2017; and Rebholz et al., 2018.

claim: Only one study has assessed the relationship between metabolomic profiling and the progression to diabetes among individuals with prediabetes and investigated the predictive values of metabolites.
source: However, we are aware of only one study that has assessed the relationship between metabolomic profiling and the progression to diabetes among individuals with prediabetes and investigated the predictive values of metabolites (Ren et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ren et al., 2021.

claim: The previous study on metabolomic profiling and diabetes progression in prediabetes was limited by a nested case–control study design with a relatively short follow-up (median 5 years) and small sample size (n = ~300).
source: Nevertheless, it was limited by a nested case–control study design with a relatively short follow-up (median 5 years) and small sample size (n = ~300).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ren et al., 2021 in the preceding sentence.

claim: The current study included 13,489 participants with prediabetes at baseline with available circulating metabolite data.
source: For the identification of metabolomic biomarkers associated with the progression from prediabetes to diabetes, the current study focused on participants with prediabetes at baseline with available circulating metabolite data.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Methods section describing the study population.

claim: Prediabetes was defined by an HbA1c level of 5.7–6.4% (39–47 mmol/mol) in participants without diabetes, according to the American Diabetes Association (ADA) criteria.
source: The diagnosis of prediabetes was defined by an HbA1c level of 5.7–6.4% (39–47 mmol/mol) in participants without diabetes, according to the American Diabetes Association (ADA) criteria (ElSayed et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to ElSayed et al., 2023, which provides the ADA criteria.

claim: After excluding individuals who developed diabetes or died within 1 month from the baseline, 13,489 participants with prediabetes were included in the final analyses.
source: After excluding individuals who developed diabetes or died within 1 month from the baseline, 13,489 participants with prediabetes were included in the final analyses.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Methods section.

claim: The metabolomics analysis of approximately 118,000 non-fasting ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) plasma samples at baseline was performed using the high-throughput NMR platform in Nightingale Health's laboratories of Finland.
source: The metabolomics analysis of approximately 118,000 non-fasting ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) plasma samples at baseline was performed using the high-throughput NMR platform in Nightingale Health's laboratories of Finland.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Methods section describing metabolite quantification.

claim: Details of the metabolic profiling platform and experimentation have been described elsewhere.
source: Details of the metabolic profiling platform and experimentation have been described elsewhere (Würtz et al., 2017; Soininen et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Würtz et al., 2017; Soininen et al., 2015; and Zhang et al., 2022.

claim: For the majority of the metabolic biomarkers, the CVs were below 5%.

claim: The distributions of measured biomarkers from five sample batches indicated absence of batch effects.
source: Furthermore, the distributions of measured biomarkers from five sample batches indicated absence of batch effects (https://biobank.ctsu.ox.ac.uk/ukb/ukb/docs/nmrm_app1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a reference to UK Biobank documentation.

claim: A total of 249 metabolic biomarkers (168 directly measured and 81 ratios of these), spanning lipids, lipoprotein subclass, fatty acids, amino acids, ketone bodies, and glycolysis metabolites were quantified for each sample.
source: A total of 249 metabolic biomarkers (168 directly measured and 81 ratios of these), spanning lipids, lipoprotein subclass, fatty acids, amino acids, ketone bodies, and glycolysis metabolites were quantified for each sample.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Methods section.

claim: In the present study, 168 metabolic biomarkers that were directly measured were analyzed.
source: In the present study, we analyzed 168 metabolic biomarkers that were directly measured (Supplementary file 1).

claim: Among the 13,489 participants with baseline prediabetes, the mean age was 59.6 (SD, 7.1) years, and 6166 (45.7%) were males.
source: Among the 13,489 participants with baseline prediabetes, the mean age was 59.6 (SD, 7.1) years, and 6166 (45.7%) were males.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: During a median follow-up of 13.6 (12.3–14.6) years, 2525 (18.7%) participants progressed to diabetes.
source: During a median follow-up of 13.6 (12.3–14.6) years, 2525 (18.7%) participants progressed to diabetes.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by the Abstract.

claim: After adjusting for covariates and correcting for multiple testing, 94 of 168 metabolic biomarkers were significantly associated with the risk of incident diabetes.
source: After adjusting for covariates and correcting for multiple testing, 94 of 168 metabolic biomarkers were significantly associated with the risk of incident diabetes (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2, showing statistical associations after adjustment.

claim: Concentrations of very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) particles, particularly larger VLDL particles and composition within larger VLDL, were strongly associated with progression to diabetes.
source: Concentrations of very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) particles, particularly larger VLDL particles and composition within larger VLDL, were strongly associated with progression to diabetes.

claim: Triglyceride in all lipoprotein subclasses demonstrated strong positive associations with diabetes risk.
source: Triglyceride in all lipoprotein subclasses also demonstrated strong positive associations with diabetes risk.

claim: Concentrations of larger high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles and composition within these particles were inversely associated with incident diabetes.
source: In contrast, concentrations of larger high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles and composition within these particles were inversely associated with incident diabetes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Larger HDL and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particle sizes were associated with a lower risk of progression to diabetes.
source: For lipoprotein particle diameter, larger HDL and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particle sizes were associated with a lower risk of progression to diabetes, while larger VLDL particle size was associated with a higher risk.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Larger VLDL particle size was associated with a higher risk of progression to diabetes.
source: For lipoprotein particle diameter, larger HDL and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particle sizes were associated with a lower risk of progression to diabetes, while larger VLDL particle size was associated with a higher risk.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Monounsaturated fatty acids and saturated fatty acids were positively associated with the risk of diabetes.
source: Monounsaturated fatty acids and saturated fatty acids were positively associated with the risk of diabetes, whereas docosahexaenoic acid and the degree of fatty acid unsaturation were negatively associated with diabetes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Docosahexaenoic acid and the degree of fatty acid unsaturation were negatively associated with diabetes.
source: Monounsaturated fatty acids and saturated fatty acids were positively associated with the risk of diabetes, whereas docosahexaenoic acid and the degree of fatty acid unsaturation were negatively associated with diabetes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Higher concentrations of alanine, tyrosine, and branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) such as leucine and valine were associated with an increased risk of diabetes.
source: Among the amino acids, higher concentrations of alanine, tyrosine, and branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) such as leucine and valine were associated with an increased risk of diabetes, but glutamine and glycine were inversely associated with diabetes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Glutamine and glycine were inversely associated with diabetes.
source: Among the amino acids, higher concentrations of alanine, tyrosine, and branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) such as leucine and valine were associated with an increased risk of diabetes, but glutamine and glycine were inversely associated with diabetes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Neither of the ketone bodies showed an association with the risk of diabetes.
source: Neither of the ketone bodies showed an association with the risk of diabetes.

claim: Of the 94 metabolites that were significantly associated with diabetes, 17 metabolites were selected by priority-Lasso.
source: Of the 94 metabolites that were significantly associated with diabetes, 17 metabolites were selected by priority-Lasso (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Supplementary file 3.

claim: The intersection of the top 20 important predictors identified by three machine-learning algorithms identified a total of 9 metabolites: cholesteryl esters in large HDL, cholesteryl esters in medium VLDL, triglycerides in very large VLDL, average diameter for LDL particles, triglycerides in intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL), glycine, tyrosine, glucose, and docosahexaenoic acid.
source: When further evaluating the importance of these metabolites after adjustment for covariates using three machine-learning algorithms, the intersection of the top 20 important predictors identified a total of 9 metabolites, namely cholesteryl esters in large HDL, cholesteryl esters in medium VLDL, triglycerides in very large VLDL, average diameter for LDL particles, triglycerides in intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL), glycine, tyrosine, glucose, and docosahexaenoic acid (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3 and Supplementary file 4.

claim: There was no obvious difference in the AUROC obtained from CPH model (1 year: 0.823 [95% CI 0.702, 0.945]; 5 years: 0.830 [0.797, 0.864]; 10 years: 0.801 [0.778, 0.825]) and RSF model (1 year: 0.828 [0.723, 0.933]; 5 years: 0.820 [0.785, 0.855]; 10 years: 0.802 [0.778, 0.826]).

claim: The addition of selected metabolites consecutively outperformed the basic model with conventional clinical variables in diabetes risk prediction from 1 to 10 years.
source: The addition of selected metabolites consecutively outperformed the basic model with conventional clinical variables in diabetes risk prediction from 1 to 10 years (Figure 4).

source: Specifically, the AUROC increased from 0.759 (95% CI 0.608, 0.911)–0.823 (0.702, 0.945), 0.798 (0.762, 0.834)–0.830 (0.797, 0.864), and 0.776 (0.750, 0.801) to 0.801 (0.778, 0.825) for 1-, 5-, and 10-year diabetes risk, respectively (Table 2 and Figure 5).

claim: Results from continuous NRI and absolute IDI demonstrated improvement in the risk prediction for progression to diabetes.
source: Results from continuous NRI and absolute IDI also demonstrated improvement in the risk prediction for progression to diabetes (Table 2)

source: although the model calibration was not significantly improved (Figure 6).

source: Compared with the low-risk group, participants in the high-risk group had a significantly higher cumulative risk of incident diabetes (log-rank p < 0.0001) (Figure 8).

claim: When participants were alternatively classified into low-, medium-, and high-risk groups according to the tertile cut-off point of the predicted value, the high-risk group showed the highest risk of developing diabetes, followed by the medium- and low-risk groups (log-rank p < 0.0001).
source: When participants were alternatively classified into low-, medium-, and high-risk groups according to the tertile cut-off point of the predicted value, the high-risk group showed the highest risk of developing diabetes, followed by the medium- and low-risk groups (log-rank p < 0.0001).

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klau et al., 2018.

claim: RSF is a machine-learning method designed to be used specifically for survival outcome prediction and has shown promising results in various settings.
source: RSF, as a machine-learning method, is designed to be used specifically for survival outcome prediction and has shown promising results in various settings (Rahman et al., 2023; Kwak et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rahman et al., 2023 and Kwak et al., 2021.

claim: RSF builds many decision trees using split points based on the log-rank test to identify different survival statuses and produces the predicted probability for an individual derived from the average prediction across all trees.
source: It builds many decision trees using split points based on the log-rank test to identify different survival statuses and produces the predicted probability for an individual derived from the average prediction across all trees (Ishwaran et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ishwaran et al., 2008.

claim: DCA calculates a clinical 'net benefit' for one or more prediction models in comparison to default strategies of treating all or no patients.
source: Furthermore, we used decision curve analysis (DCA) to assess the clinical usefulness of prediction model-based guidance for prediabetes management, which calculates a clinical 'net benefit' for one or more prediction models in comparison to default strategies of treating all or no patients (Vickers et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vickers et al., 2019.

claim: A model with good discrimination does not necessarily have high clinical value.
source: Most importantly, a model with good discrimination does not necessarily have high clinical value.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge in the field of prediction modeling.

claim: The addition of the metabolites increased the clinical value of prediction, that is, the potential benefit of guiding management in individuals with prediabetes.
source: Hence, DCA was used to compare the clinical utility of the model before and after adding the metabolites, and this showed a higher net benefit for the latter than the basic model, suggesting the addition of the metabolites increased the clinical value of prediction, that is, the potential benefit of guiding management in individuals with prediabetes (Vickers et al., 2019; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the DCA results in Figure 7, with citations to Vickers et al., 2019 and Li et al., 2023.

claim: Even a modest improvement in diabetes risk prediction among individuals with prediabetes will have substantial clinical and public health implications.
source: Considering the epidemic proportion of prediabetes worldwide, even a modest improvement in diabetes risk prediction among individuals with prediabetes will have substantial clinical and public health implications.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as an inference based on the large population affected by prediabetes.
